newsitem.title: GERMANY: EC official backs special EMU deal for Germany.
newsitem.headline: EC official backs special EMU deal for Germany.

text.p: European Commissioner Monika Wulf Mathies on Friday weighed into a debate on the entry criteria to Europe's monetary union, suggesting Germany should receive special treatment because of unification.
The costs of Germany's unification need to be considered "as a very important aspect" at next year's Maastricht test, Wulf Mathies told German newspaper Berliner Morgenpost.

Wulf Mathies, formerly the head of Germany's public service sector union OeTV, commented at a time German politicians are insisting Germany would still meet the strict fiscal criteria to join the currency union at its launch in January 1999.

If Germany should fail to meet the stability criteria the Treaty would justify an exemption due to exceptional circumstances, Wulf Mathies said, noting that without the costs of unification, Germany's fiscal data would "look quite different."
Currently a number of nations, including Germany, are struggling to meet the strict entry criteria.
At the same time however Finance Minister Theo Waigel is calling for an extra tough interpretation of the fiscal criteria.
He is demanding that the Treaty's conditions that a nation's budget deficit not exceed three percent of gross domestic product should actually mean that budget deficits may not top 3.0 percent.
The Bonn government still predicts its 1997 budget deficit will total 2.9 percent of gross domestic product even though independent economists say it could be higher, closer to 3.2 percent.
Wulf Mathies also said there was still a realistic chance that Germany would be able to fulfil the criteria on time without making use of special measures.
But Wulf Mathies lashed out at Bonn for what she called "percentage point acrobatics," and stressed that meeting the criteria did not mean these goals must be fulfilled to the decimal point.
"The number 3.0 percent is not written in the Maastricht Treaty, the currency union is not some numbers lottery but rather a conscious political decision," she told the newspaper.
A summary of the article was made available before publication.

Wulf Mathies said that Germany's hardline stance "no longer had anything in common with economic sense" and stressed that the Treaty did not envision postponing the launch date if the budget deficit reached 3.2 percent.

The commissioner also said postponing the launch of the currency union would be detrimental for Germany as a delay could trigger new currency market turbulence which could hurt Germany's export driven economy and in the end lead to further job losses.
Wulf Mathies supported a proposal put forward by IG Metall union head Klaus Zwickel that new jobs could be created by curbing the working week to 32 hours.
